questions.question: A plain binary search tree receives the keys 1, 2, 3, ..., 4000 in that order. What is its height afterwards?
options: About 12, since log2(4000) is about 12
About 24, twice the optimal height
4000, because every key becomes a right child
About 64, one level per bit of the key
questions.explanation: Each new key is larger than every existing key, so it is attached as the rightmost node and the tree is a linked list of height n. Sorted keys are the normal case for timestamps and sequence numbers, which is why balancing is not optional.

questions.question: An AVL tree receives 30, then 10, then 20. Which case is triggered at the root, and how many rotations fix it?
options: LL: one right rotation at 30
LR: a left rotation at 10, then a right rotation at 30
RL: a right rotation at 20, then a left rotation at 30
RR: one left rotation at 30
questions.explanation: After inserting 20 the root 30 has balance +2 and its left child 10 leans right (balance -1), the zig-zag LR shape. Rotating left at 10 straightens it into LL, then rotating right at 30 balances it; the test asserts rotations == 2. LL would apply only if 20 were under 10's left.

questions.question: In the red-black insert fix-up, the new red node's parent is red and its uncle is also red. What happens?
options: Rotate at the grandparent, then recolour the parent and grandparent to restore black height
Rotate at the parent so the zig-zag becomes a straight line, then rotate at the grandparent
Recolour parent and uncle black and grandparent red, then continue from the grandparent
Colour the new node black instead of red so the red-red edge disappears without rotating
questions.explanation: This is case 1: recolouring pushes the red up two levels without changing any black height, and the loop continues because the grandparent may now have a red parent. Rotations are reserved for a black uncle (cases 2 and 3). Colouring the new node black would add a black to its paths and break property 5.

questions.question: Why is a red-black tree's height at most 2 log2(n+1)?
options: Every insert performs at most two rotations, so the depth of any leaf grows by at most two per insert
Every path has the same black count and no two reds are adjacent, so no path exceeds twice the black height
Half of all nodes are red, and red nodes do not count towards the height that the bound measures
Each rotation halves the height of the subtree it touches, so the tree stays within a factor of two
questions.explanation: Property 5 gives every root-to-leaf path the same black height bh, property 4 caps reds at one per black, so paths have at most 2bh nodes; an all-black tree of black height bh has 2^bh - 1 nodes, so bh <= log2(n+1). Rotation counts bound update cost, not height.

questions.question: On 100,000 random inserts the demo measured AVL height 20 with 69,356 rotations and red-black height 20 with 57,968 rotations plus 231,220 recolourings. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Red-black is slower because it performs more total operations
AVL should always be preferred because its worst-case height bound is lower
Red-black does less pointer work per update, which is why update-heavy libraries chose it
The two trees are equivalent and the choice is a matter of taste
questions.explanation: A recolouring is a one-byte write; a rotation rewrites three pointers and invalidates cache lines. Fewer rotations with cheap recolourings is exactly the trade TreeMap, std::map, and the Linux scheduler made. AVL's lower height bound matters for lookup-dominated workloads, not always.

questions.question: A hold-expiry sweeper needs 'all holds expiring before now' every second, for 4 million holds. Which structure and operation fit?
options: A HashMap keyed by hold id, scanned fully each second
An ordered tree keyed by expiry, using range or pollFirstEntry from the smallest key
A HashMap keyed by expiry instant, looked up for each possible millisecond
A plain BST keyed by expiry, since expiries arrive in random order
questions.explanation: Range and predecessor queries are what ordered trees provide and hash maps cannot; the sweep costs O(log n + k) for k expired holds. A full scan is O(n) per second, a per-millisecond lookup is O(window), and a plain BST degenerates because expiries arrive in nearly sorted order.
